core: Simile as an explicit comparison using a marker such as like, as, or than
The simile/metaphor distinction (explicit marker versus implicit identity)
Effects similes can create: clarity, vividness, surprise, defamiliarization
Analyzing a simile's tenor and vehicle and why the comparison is apt or revealing
The epic (Homeric) simile as an extended, developed comparison
Common pitfalls: clichéd similes and mixed comparisons
supporting: The ground of a comparison (shared attributes between tenor and vehicle)
Figurative language as an analysis category affecting meaning and tone
The historical provenance of tenor/vehicle (I. A. Richards, 1936) and defamiliarization (Viktor Shklovsky, 1917)
outOfScope: Metaphor as a topic in its own right (implicit comparison is stated crisply, then the lesson moves on)

claims.claim: A simile is an explicit figure of speech that compares two different things using a marker such as 'like,' 'as,' or 'than,' which keeps the two items of the comparison visible.
A metaphor makes its comparison implicitly, by referring to one thing as another without a marker such as 'like' or 'as'; a comparison that includes such a marker is called a simile.
Besides 'like' and 'as,' some documented definitions of simile include 'than,' 'appears,' or 'seems' as possible comparison markers.
In textual analysis, figurative language such as simile, metaphor, and personification is treated as a category of authorial choice whose effect on meaning, tone, and audience is examined.

The two parts of a comparison are the tenor, the subject to which attributes are ascribed, and the vehicle, the object whose attributes are borrowed; the terms come from I. A. Richards, The Philosophy of Rhetoric (1936).
An epic, or Homeric, simile is an extended simile often running to several lines, used typically in epic poetry to intensify the heroic stature of the subject and to serve as decoration.
Defamiliarization, a term coined by Viktor Shklovsky in 1917, describes the artistic effect of making the familiar strange so that it is perceived freshly; a fresh comparison can create this effect.
A mixed metaphor (or mixed comparison) combines inconsistent or incongruous images, so a reader cannot tell which quality is being borrowed; coherent writing keeps one comparison running.
Comparisons can wear out: words and phrases that were once vivid figures can become dead figures whose original aptness has been lost, which is why clichéd similes no longer clarify or surprise.
Figurative language is often used to create a memorable image for the reader, which underlies the clarifying and vivid effects commonly attributed to similes.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Definitions differ on which words can mark a simile.
positions: Some glossaries restrict the markers to 'like' and 'as' (Pima Open Literary Terms Definition List; Purdue OWL Literary Terms).
Other definitions include 'than,' and some add 'appears' or 'seems' (Poetry Foundation glossary; eCampusOntario English for Degree Entrance).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents 'like,' 'as,' and 'than' as the standard documented markers, notes that some definitions add 'appears' or 'seems,' and avoids claiming one exclusive list.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Simile is sometimes treated as a subtype of metaphor and sometimes as an independent figure.
positions: Some rhetorical traditions treat metaphor as the broad category and simile as an explicit variant (Silva Rhetoricae calls simile an explicit comparison and lists metaphor as its related figure).
Textbook definitions distinguish the two as separate figures defined by the presence or absence of a marker (Pima; Purdue OWL; Britannica).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the marker-based textbook distinction while noting the close relationship: both compare unlike things, and the marker is the deciding feature.
